6	## Context
7	Iteration 03 was accepted (`iter-03`). I2C_SGL, I2C_AD0/1/2 and I2C_TEST are in place, and the mock emulates an I2C bus of `MockI2cDevice`s.
8

15	**Page numbers.** Every page number below is the datasheet's printed page, which is also the PDF page. NEXT 03's I2C page numbers were one page low; requirement 7 corrects them.
16	
17	## Goal
18	`usb_iss_app.iss` can build I2C_DIRECT frames from sub-commands, refuse frames that break the limits, send them, and parse the two status bytes and the data. The mock interprets I2C_DIRECT against its `MockI2cDevice`s. On hardware, address-only frames on the empty bus, an unknown sub-command and the frame-length boundary record what the real device answers.
19	
20	## Requirements
21	
22	### 1. Constants (p.15; D-007)
23	- `I2C_DIRECT = 0x57`.
24	- Sub-commands:
25	  - `I2C_DIRECT_START = 0x01`, `I2C_DIRECT_RESTART = 0x02`, `I2C_DIRECT_STOP = 0x03`, `I2C_DIRECT_NACK = 0x04`;
26	  - READ is `0x20`–`0x2F` and WRITE is `0x30`–`0x3F`.
27	- `I2C_DIRECT_FRAME_MAX = 59` (D-007: the whole frame, `0x57` included). `I2C_DIRECT_CHUNK_MAX = 16` (p.15). `I2C_DIRECT_READ_TOTAL_MAX = 60` (D-007). Cite the page or D-007 in a comment on each.
28	- `I2C_DIRECT_NACK_REASONS = {0x01: "Device Error", 0x02: "Buffer Overflow", 0x03: "Buffer Underflow", 0x04: "Unknown command"}` (p.15).
29	- `IssNack`: when `command == "I2C_DIRECT"`, take the reason's name from `I2C_DIRECT_NACK_REASONS`, not from `NACK_REASONS`.
30	  - The message reads, for example, `"I2C_DIRECT NACK: 0x01 Device Error"`.
31	  - ISS_MODE messages don't change.
32	  - Update the docstring.
33	
34	### 2. Builders (p.15)
35	- `direct_read(n) -> bytes` returns `bytes([0x20 + n - 1])`. It raises `ValueError` unless 1 ≤ n ≤ 16.
36	- `direct_write(data) -> bytes` returns `bytes([0x30 + len(data) - 1]) + data`. It raises `ValueError` unless 1 ≤ len(data) ≤ 16.
37	- `build_i2c_direct(*parts: int | bytes) -> bytes` returns `57` followed by the parts. An `int` part is one sub-command byte (0–255); a `bytes` part is appended as is.
38	  - It then walks the sub-commands and raises `ValueError` if:
39	    - there are none;
40	    - a sub-command byte is not in `01`–`04`, `20`–`2F` or `30`–`3F`;
41	    - a WRITE is followed by fewer data bytes than its count;
42	    - the frame is longer than 59 bytes;
43	    - the READ counts add up to more than 60.
44	  - It does not check I2C semantics, such as whether a START comes before an address.
45	  - The device address is written with a WRITE like any other byte. In the p.15 example, `31 40 55` is WRITE 2: address `40`, then data `55`.
46	- `i2c_direct_read_count(frame: bytes) -> int` returns the total READ bytes in a built frame, using the same walk.
47	
48	### 3. Parser and helper (p.15)
49	- `parse_i2c_direct_status(resp: bytes) -> int`:
50	  - fewer than 2 bytes → `IssTimeout`;
51	  - `00 rr` → `IssNack(rr, "I2C_DIRECT")`;
52	  - `FF nn` → returns `nn`;
53	  - any other first byte → `IssProtocolError`.
54	- `i2c_direct(t, *parts) -> bytes`:
55	  - builds the frame and sends it in **one** `write()` call (D-007);
56	  - reads 2 bytes and parses them;
57	  - reads `nn` bytes; fewer → `IssTimeout`;
58	  - if `nn` differs from `i2c_direct_read_count(frame)` → `IssProtocolError` (after reading the `nn` bytes, so nothing is left behind);
59	  - returns the data;
60	  - uses the transport's default 500 ms timeout, as for the other I2C commands (pp.11–14).
61	
62	### 4. Builder and parser tests
63	- Exact bytes for every datasheet example, built with the builders:
64	  - `57 01 31 40 55 03` (p.15, PCF8574 write);
65	  - `57 01 34 A0 00 00 12 34 03` (p.16, 24LC512 write, with `nn nn` = `12 34`);
66	  - `57 01 32 A0 00 00 02 30 A1 22 04 20 03` (p.16, 4-byte read with NACK); read count 4;
67	  - `57 01 32 A0 00 00 02 30 A1 23 03` (p.16, 4-byte read); read count 4.
68	- Every limit at the boundary and one past it:
69	  - `direct_read`: 16 and 1 are accepted; 17 and 0 are refused;
70	  - `direct_write`: 16 and 1 bytes are accepted; 17 bytes and empty are refused;
71	  - frame length: 58 × `I2C_DIRECT_STOP` (59 bytes) is accepted; 59 × (60 bytes) is refused;
72	  - total read: `direct_read(16)` × 3 + `direct_read(12)` (60) is accepted; with `direct_read(13)` instead (61) it is refused.
73	- Also refused: no parts; sub-command bytes `00`, `05`, `1F` and `40`; `build_i2c_direct(0x31, b"\x40")` (WRITE 2 with one data byte); an int part of 256.
74	- Parser:
75	  - `FF 00` → 0; `FF 04` → 4;
76	  - `00 01` to `00 04` → `IssNack` with that `reason`, and with the name from the table in its message;
77	  - `00` alone and empty → `IssTimeout`;
78	  - `7F 00` → `IssProtocolError`.
79	
80	### 5. Mock: I2C_DIRECT (SPEC §3, "the mock"; pp.15–16; D-007)
81	- **Device model.** `MockI2cDevice` gains `addr_bytes: int = 1` (0, 1 or 2). Only I2C_DIRECT uses it:
82	  - in a write transaction, the first `addr_bytes` bytes after the address set the pointer, high byte first, once all of them have arrived;
83	  - later bytes are written at the pointer.
84	
85	  I2C_SGL, I2C_AD0, I2C_AD1 and I2C_AD2 behave as before.
86	- **Framing (D-007).** When `0x57` is at the head of the buffer, the frame is everything from it to the end of the bytes received in that `write()` call. The mock does not wait for a later `write()`, just as for SERIAL_IO.
87	- **In the I2C modes and I2C+SERIAL:**
88	  - A frame longer than 59 bytes → `00 02`, and nothing is executed.
89	  - Otherwise, walk the sub-commands in order:
90	    - START or RESTART: the next byte written is an address.
91	    - WRITE k: if fewer than k bytes remain → `00 03`, and stop.
92	      - If an address is expected, the first byte is the address, and the device is `i2c_devices.get(b & 0xFE)`. If it is absent → `00 01`, and stop. ASSUMPTION: the device stops at the first unacknowledged address. The address's low bit selects write or read.
93	      - The other bytes go to the device addressed for writing (pointer bytes, then data, as above). If no device is addressed for writing, they are discarded.
94	    - READ k: k bytes from the device addressed for reading, appended to the read buffer. If no device is addressed for reading → k × `FF`. ASSUMPTION: the pull-ups hold SDA high, which matches iteration 03's empty-bus read.
95	    - NACK has no effect in the mock. STOP ends the transaction, so the next address needs a START.
96	    - Any other byte → `00 04`, and stop.
97	  - At the end of the frame → `FF n` followed by the n bytes read.
98	  - The mock does not check the total read count; the builder refuses those frames.
99	- **Other modes** (IO_MODE, IO_MODE+SERIAL, SPI): consume the frame, record it in `unhandled`, and send no reply. ASSUMPTION; hardware step 5 records IO_MODE.

101	  - p.15 example against a device at `0x40` with `addr_bytes=0`: returns `b""`, and `mem[0] == 0x55`.

104	  - Absent address → `IssNack` with reason 1.
105	  - Raw `57 01 31 40` in one `write()` → `00 03`.
106	  - Raw `57 05` → `00 04`.
107	  - Raw `57` + 59 × `03` (60 bytes) → `00 02`. Raw `57` + 58 × `03` (59 bytes) → `FF 00`.
108	  - Split frame: raw `57 01 31` → `00 03` straight away. A following raw `40 55 03` gets no reply, and its bytes are in `unhandled`.
109	  - `5A 01` inside WRITE data is stored as data: no ISS_VERSION reply, and `unhandled` stays empty.
110	  - The commands work in I2C+SERIAL.
111	  - In IO_MODE, `i2c_direct` raises `IssTimeout`, the frame is in `unhandled`, and a following `version()` answers mode 0x00.
112

116	- Change `test_i2c.py::test_mock_io_mode_consumes_frame`:
117	  - `i2c_test` now returns `False`, and `58 A0` is not in `unhandled`;
118	  - the AD1-write half of the test stays as it is.

121	- Add a test: in IO_MODE+SERIAL, `i2c_test` still raises `IssTimeout`, and the frame is in `unhandled`.

126	- `pp.10-13` → `pp.11-14`, and `pp.10-15` → `pp.11-16`.

128	- p.3 (pull-ups) is already correct.

131	Change only `tests/test_hw.py::test_hw_mode_sequence`:
132	- I2C mode IO_TYPE `0x0A` → `0xAA`, in both the set and the restore, and in their labels.

138	- No SPI command (iteration 05). No GUI.
139	- No data byte written to any I2C address on hardware (see below).
140	- Do not edit SPEC, DECISIONS, HARDWARE, the role files, the templates, LOG or CHANGES.

147	- SCL and SDA (I/O3 and I/O4) are **not connected**. In the I2C modes the board's 4.7k pull-ups hold the bus high; in the other modes they are disconnected (p.3).

# NEXT — Iteration 04 (fix cycle 0)

Recommended model/effort: Sonnet 5.5, high. The I2C_DIRECT sub-command interpreter in the mock is the most involved mock work so far.
Author: revclaude. Read `docs/iterations/03/review.md` first. Requirements 6–8 carry over from it.

## Context
Iteration 03 was accepted (`iter-03`). I2C_SGL, I2C_AD0/1/2 and I2C_TEST are in place, and the mock emulates an I2C bus of `MockI2cDevice`s.

This iteration is **the first half of roadmap item 04** (SPEC §6: "I2C_DIRECT and SPI"). It covers **I2C_DIRECT** only (datasheet pp.15–16). SPI is iteration 05. From now on, roadmap items 05–10 run two iteration numbers later than their labels.

The limits and the framing rule follow **D-007** (pending claude1).

A claude1 checkpoint is due (4 accepted iterations). Chris decides whether this build waits for it.

**Page numbers.** Every page number below is the datasheet's printed page, which is also the PDF page. NEXT 03's I2C page numbers were one page low; requirement 7 corrects them.

## Goal
`usb_iss_app.iss` can build I2C_DIRECT frames from sub-commands, refuse frames that break the limits, send them, and parse the two status bytes and the data. The mock interprets I2C_DIRECT against its `MockI2cDevice`s. On hardware, address-only frames on the empty bus, an unknown sub-command and the frame-length boundary record what the real device answers.

## Requirements

### 1. Constants (p.15; D-007)
- `I2C_DIRECT = 0x57`.
- Sub-commands:
  - `I2C_DIRECT_START = 0x01`, `I2C_DIRECT_RESTART = 0x02`, `I2C_DIRECT_STOP = 0x03`, `I2C_DIRECT_NACK = 0x04`;
  - READ is `0x20`–`0x2F` and WRITE is `0x30`–`0x3F`.
- `I2C_DIRECT_FRAME_MAX = 59` (D-007: the whole frame, `0x57` included). `I2C_DIRECT_CHUNK_MAX = 16` (p.15). `I2C_DIRECT_READ_TOTAL_MAX = 60` (D-007). Cite the page or D-007 in a comment on each.
- `I2C_DIRECT_NACK_REASONS = {0x01: "Device Error", 0x02: "Buffer Overflow", 0x03: "Buffer Underflow", 0x04: "Unknown command"}` (p.15).
- `IssNack`: when `command == "I2C_DIRECT"`, take the reason's name from `I2C_DIRECT_NACK_REASONS`, not from `NACK_REASONS`.
  - The message reads, for example, `"I2C_DIRECT NACK: 0x01 Device Error"`.
  - ISS_MODE messages don't change.
  - Update the docstring.

### 2. Builders (p.15)
- `direct_read(n) -> bytes` returns `bytes([0x20 + n - 1])`. It raises `ValueError` unless 1 ≤ n ≤ 16.
- `direct_write(data) -> bytes` returns `bytes([0x30 + len(data) - 1]) + data`. It raises `ValueError` unless 1 ≤ len(data) ≤ 16.
- `build_i2c_direct(*parts: int | bytes) -> bytes` returns `57` followed by the parts. An `int` part is one sub-command byte (0–255); a `bytes` part is appended as is.
  - It then walks the sub-commands and raises `ValueError` if:
    - there are none;
    - a sub-command byte is not in `01`–`04`, `20`–`2F` or `30`–`3F`;
    - a WRITE is followed by fewer data bytes than its count;
    - the frame is longer than 59 bytes;
    - the READ counts add up to more than 60.
  - It does not check I2C semantics, such as whether a START comes before an address.
  - The device address is written with a WRITE like any other byte. In the p.15 example, `31 40 55` is WRITE 2: address `40`, then data `55`.
- `i2c_direct_read_count(frame: bytes) -> int` returns the total READ bytes in a built frame, using the same walk.

### 3. Parser and helper (p.15)
- `parse_i2c_direct_status(resp: bytes) -> int`:
  - fewer than 2 bytes → `IssTimeout`;
  - `00 rr` → `IssNack(rr, "I2C_DIRECT")`;
  - `FF nn` → returns `nn`;
  - any other first byte → `IssProtocolError`.
- `i2c_direct(t, *parts) -> bytes`:
  - builds the frame and sends it in **one** `write()` call (D-007);
  - reads 2 bytes and parses them;
  - reads `nn` bytes; fewer → `IssTimeout`;
  - if `nn` differs from `i2c_direct_read_count(frame)` → `IssProtocolError` (after reading the `nn` bytes, so nothing is left behind);
  - returns the data;
  - uses the transport's default 500 ms timeout, as for the other I2C commands (pp.11–14).

### 4. Builder and parser tests
- Exact bytes for every datasheet example, built with the builders:
  - `57 01 31 40 55 03` (p.15, PCF8574 write);
  - `57 01 34 A0 00 00 12 34 03` (p.16, 24LC512 write, with `nn nn` = `12 34`);
  - `57 01 32 A0 00 00 02 30 A1 22 04 20 03` (p.16, 4-byte read with NACK); read count 4;
  - `57 01 32 A0 00 00 02 30 A1 23 03` (p.16, 4-byte read); read count 4.
- Every limit at the boundary and one past it:
  - `direct_read`: 16 and 1 are accepted; 17 and 0 are refused;
  - `direct_write`: 16 and 1 bytes are accepted; 17 bytes and empty are refused;
  - frame length: 58 × `I2C_DIRECT_STOP` (59 bytes) is accepted; 59 × (60 bytes) is refused;
  - total read: `direct_read(16)` × 3 + `direct_read(12)` (60) is accepted; with `direct_read(13)` instead (61) it is refused.
- Also refused: no parts; sub-command bytes `00`, `05`, `1F` and `40`; `build_i2c_direct(0x31, b"\x40")` (WRITE 2 with one data byte); an int part of 256.
- Parser:
  - `FF 00` → 0; `FF 04` → 4;
  - `00 01` to `00 04` → `IssNack` with that `reason`, and with the name from the table in its message;
  - `00` alone and empty → `IssTimeout`;

## Attached: GY-MCU90640, serial mode (card `gy-mcu90640`, mode `serial`)

| GY pin | Connects to | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| VIN | separate 5 V supply (measured 5.0 V) | 100 nF (104) capacitor across VIN and GND. 42 mA draw. |
| GND | supply GND **and** USB-ISS GND | Common ground. |
| TX | USB-ISS I/O1 | USB-ISS RX in serial modes. **Driven by the module**, 3.3 V high (measured). |
| RX | USB-ISS I/O2 | USB-ISS TX in serial modes. 3.3 V logic on both sides. |
| SCL, SDA | not connected | These pins are the MLX90640's own I2C bus. With PS open, the module's MCU is the master on that bus. Never connect them to the USB-ISS in this mode. |

### Consequences for tests
- I/O1 is driven by the module's TX. At power-up the module transmits continuously at 115200 baud, as confirmed on a scope (2026-10-17). **Never configure I/O1 as an output.** In IO_MODE, GETPINS and GETAD on I/O1 return varying values, including `00 00` when sampled while TX is low. - While I/O2 is an input, the RX line is undriven. It sits near 2.4 V and picks up crosstalk from TX (scope, 2026-10-17). This is harmless, and in serial modes the USB-ISS drives it.
- In serial modes the USB-ISS drives I/O2 (TX) into the module's RX. Any byte sent is a command to the module (GY manual §IV). Send only commands that `NEXT.md` names explicitly. Never send save-to-flash in automated tests (SPEC §7).
- I/O3 and I/O4 (SCL and SDA in I2C modes) are unconnected. The I2C bus is empty, and the USB-ISS's 4.7k pull-ups hold it at 3.3 V.
- In every IO_TYPE byte, set unused pin pairs to digital input (`10`), never output (`00`/`01`).

# Bench hardware

Chris owns this file. It describes what is physically connected to the USB-ISS right now. Read it before any hardware test. A `NEXT.md` hardware section must be consistent with it. If they disagree, stop and report the conflict.

Last updated: 2026-10-17 (claude1, from Chris's measurements). **Bench changed after iteration 02:** the USB-ISS now runs at 3.3 V. Hardware logs from iterations 00–02 were taken at 5 V.

## USB-ISS
- Connected to the PC over USB, which also powers it. The port comes from `USB_ISS_PORT` in `.env`.
- **The 5 V power link is removed, so the USB-ISS runs at 3.3 V.** VCC measured 3.3 V. Logic levels are 3.3 V. Inputs are **not** 5 V tolerant (datasheet p.3).
- The bootloader link is not fitted. Never fit it.
- The VCC pin is **not connected** to anything. Never apply an external voltage to it (p.3).
- GETAD full scale (1023) now corresponds to 3.3 V.
- The bench unit is firmware 0x09, serial 00069221, and `.env` points to it.
- A second USB-ISS, serial 00069220 (firmware 0x09), is available but not normally connected. It was used once in iteration 02 to cross-check the GETAD erratum.
- **The `.env` setting is copied into each VS Code terminal when the terminal opens** (`python.terminal.useEnvFile`), and the environment variable takes priority over `.env`. After you edit `.env`, open a new terminal. To use a different port for one run, set it on the command line: `USB_ISS_PORT=... <command>`.

## Attached: GY-MCU90640, serial mode (card `gy-mcu90640`, mode `serial`)

| GY pin | Connects to | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| VIN | separate 5 V supply (measured 5.0 V) | 100 nF (104) capacitor across VIN and GND. 42 mA draw. |
| GND | supply GND **and** USB-ISS GND | Common ground. |
| TX | USB-ISS I/O1 | USB-ISS RX in serial modes. **Driven by the module**, 3.3 V high (measured). |
| RX | USB-ISS I/O2 | USB-ISS TX in serial modes. 3.3 V logic on both sides. |
| SCL, SDA | not connected | These pins are the MLX90640's own I2C bus. With PS open, the module's MCU is the master on that bus. Never connect them to the USB-ISS in this mode. |
| PS | open | Serial mode. Grounding PS and power-cycling selects I2C-direct mode (GY manual p.5). |

### Consequences for tests
- I/O1 is driven by the module's TX. At power-up the module transmits continuously at 115200 baud, as confirmed on a scope (2026-10-17). **Never configure I/O1 as an output.** In IO_MODE, GETPINS and GETAD on I/O1 return varying values, including `00 00` when sampled while TX is low. Log them, don't assert them.
- While I/O2 is an input, the RX line is undriven. It sits near 2.4 V and picks up crosstalk from TX (scope, 2026-10-17). This is harmless, and in serial modes the USB-ISS drives it.
- In serial modes the USB-ISS drives I/O2 (TX) into the module's RX. Any byte sent is a command to the module (GY manual §IV). Send only commands that `NEXT.md` names explicitly. Never send save-to-flash in automated tests (SPEC §7).
- I/O3 and I/O4 (SCL and SDA in I2C modes) are unconnected. The I2C bus is empty, and the USB-ISS's 4.7k pull-ups hold it at 3.3 V.
- In every IO_TYPE byte, set unused pin pairs to digital input (`10`), never output (`00`/`01`).

## Not attached
- A second GY-MCU90640 with PS grounded (I2C direct). It was removed on 2026-10-17 because two modules would exceed the 80 mA power budget. Iteration 01's hardware runs were taken with both modules attached and the I2C lines shared.

The I2C_DIRECT commands are used to build custom I2C sequences. You send the I2C_DIRECT command (0x57)
followed by as many sub-commands as required.
These sub-commands are:

START             0x01             send start sequence
RESTART           0x02             send restart sequence
STOP              0x03             send stop sequence
NACK              0x04             send NACK after next read
READ              0x20 - 0x2F      reads 1-16 bytes
WRITE             0x30 - 0x3F      writes next 1-16 bytes


The I2C_Read sub-commands can read up to 16 bytes. 0x20 will read 1 byte, 0x21 will read 2 bytes, 0x2F will read 16
bytes. All bytes read are buffered and sent after all sub-commands are processed.
The I2C_Write sub-commands can write up to 16 bytes. 0x30 will write 1 byte, 0x35 will write 6 bytes, 0x3F will write
16 bytes. The bytes to be written immediately follow the write sub-command.
It is up to you to make sure you supply the correct number of bytes as specified in the sub-command.
The response to the I2C_DIRECT command is a variable number of bytes, but it will always be at least two. You should
read these two bytes first as they are the status bytes.
The fist byte is the ACK (0xFF) or NACK (0x00) status.
If you get an ACK the command was successful and the second byte contains the number of bytes to read. If you have
not requested any reads then it will be zero, otherwise you should now read the number of bytes available.
If you get a NACK the command failed and the second byte contains the reason, as follows:

Error Type                 Error Code       Comment
Device Error               0x01             No ACK from device
Buffer Overflow            0x02             You must limit the frame to < 60 bytes
Buffer Underflow           0x03             More write data was expected than sent
Unknown command            0x04             Probably your write count is wrong

RESTART           0x02             send restart sequence

WRITE             0x30 - 0x3F      writes next 1-16 bytes
